summary: A short note on vitamin B12 (cobalamin) chemistry and environmental mercury poisoning. It explains that methylcobalamin can react with Hg(II) to form the more toxic methylmercury ion, CH3Hg+, which occurs naturally in sediments but is greatly worsened by human mercury release. It recounts the Minamata Bay disaster in Japan, where a chemical company's dumping caused methylmercury poisoning through contaminated fish, and notes a later mercury problem among gold miners on Amazon tributaries.
one_line: Explains how vitamin B12 chemistry produces toxic methylmercury and recounts the Minamata Bay poisoning disaster and later Amazon gold-mining mercury contamination.
key_facts: Methyl-cobalamin, one of the cobalamin compounds, can react with less poisonous Hg(II) to generate the more poisonous ion CH3Hg+.
Humans can greatly worsen the mercury problem by releasing mercury and organomercurials into the environment.
There is a natural level of methylmercury formed by conversion of Hg(II) into CH3Hg+ in sediments.
Anyone eating fish is likely to have an increased level of methylmercurials in their body.
Wood proposed in 1968 that methylmercury could form from methylcobalamin, following model reactions of MeCo(CN)5 3+ and Hg(II) by Halpern and Maher.
The cyanocobaltates were among the first cobalamin models, discovered slightly before the cobaloximes studied by Schrauzer.
The worst episode of methylmercury poisoning occurred in Minamata Bay in Japan, devastating local fishermen and their families.
From the 1930's to the 1960's, a chemical company dumped tons of mercury into Minamata Bay in Japan.
Thousands of people living around Minamata Bay developed methylmercury poisoning through eating contaminated fish.
The disorder caused by Minamata poisoning became known as Minamata Disease.
Minamata Disease symptoms may include tingling sensations, muscle weakness, unsteady gait, tunnel vision, slurred speech, hearing loss, and abnormal behaviour such as sudden fits of laughter.
The note recommends reading the statement from the Tokyo Exposition of 1996 by Saburo Horikawa.
Mercury poisoning problems are currently occurring with gold miners working on tributaries of the Amazon.
